notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the Trojans' fatal act happen before our eyes.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The first word shows the Trojans themselves tearing open the walls that the Greeks had failed to break in ten years.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: The horse was too large to pass through the gates of Troy

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: Another present tense keeps the scene vivid and fast.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.trans: we lay open the walls of the city
notes.body: The verb sits between "walls" and "of the city", so the word order itself opens up the walls, as the Trojans do.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense shows the eager work going on now.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Opening with the verb stresses how keen the Trojans are to begin their own destruction.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: Everyone joins in: the whole city shares the blame, which deepens the tragedy.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the practical details vivid, as if we were watching the work.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense keeps the action moving towards the moment the horse enters.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb is pushed to the start of the line, so the effort of hauling the horse is felt.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The horse climbs the walls in the present tense, like an enemy soldier scaling them.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes first, so the horse is pictured scaling the walls like an attacker in a siege.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The walls, Troy's defences, end the sentence: the horse now crosses them.

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: feta means "pregnant": the horse carries armed men like a mother carrying young, a grim image of what it will soon release.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The horse's deadly contents are held over to the next line and placed first, so the reader is jolted by the truth the Trojans cannot see.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the children's singing vivid, which makes the scene even more tragic.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: Ending on "they rejoice" shows the innocent joy of the children as they pull their own city's doom.

notes.label: Dramatic irony
notes.body: The children are happy to touch the rope, but the reader knows they are helping to destroy Troy.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense and the gliding verb echo the snakes, so the horse seems to slither into the city just as they did.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.trans: into the middle of the city
notes.body: The words for "middle" and "city" frame the threatening horse as it glides into the heart of Troy.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: Aeneas breaks off his story to cry out to Troy itself, which shows how painful the memory still is for him.

notes.label: Apostrophe
notes.body: The repeated cry addresses the city by its ancient name and calls it the home of the gods, which makes its fall all the more terrible.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: The adjective and noun are split across the line, stressing the walls' past glory just as they are betrayed.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three addresses build to a climax of grief, as Aeneas calls out to his city again and again.

notes.label: Elision
notes.body: The vowels run together, which speeds the line as the horse reaches the gate.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb comes at the start of the line, after the pause of the line end, so the horse seems to stop dead on the threshold.

notes.label: Perfect tense
notes.body: After the run of present tenses, the perfect substitit marks a sudden halt, a moment that should have warned the Trojans.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: To stumble on the threshold was always held as a bad omen

notes.label: Metaphor
notes.body: uterus means "womb", continuing the image of the pregnant horse about to give birth to soldiers.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: quater is repeated, so the reader counts the warnings the Trojans ignore.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: it stopped, and in its belly four times a sound
notes.body: The repeated s and t sounds imitate the clank of the armour inside the horse.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: arma comes late in the sentence, so the truth about what is inside arrives at the end, when it is almost too late.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The first word shows the Trojans pushing ahead even after the warnings.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense brings the reader back into the action and the mistake.

notes.label: Madness
notes.body: furor (madness) is a key idea in the Aeneid: the Trojans are blinded and cannot see what is plain in front of them.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the final mistake vivid: the Trojans themselves place their doom in the heart of the city.

notes.label: Juxtaposition
notes.body: The ill-omened monster is placed right next to the holy citadel, which makes the contrast stark.

notes.label: Sibilance
notes.body: The repeated s sounds give the line a hissing sound that echoes the snakes.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: The holy citadel surrounds the verb, so the monster is set right in the middle of Troy's holiest place.

notes.label: Ilium
notes.body: Another name for Troy, from Ilus, one of its early kings. Aeneas calls it the home of the gods because gods were said to have helped build its walls: Apollo and Neptune built them for King Laomedon.

notes.label: The Trojans
notes.body: The Dardanidae are the descendants of Dardanus, son of Jupiter and founder of the Trojan royal family, from whom Aeneas himself was descended.

notes.label: Hymns
notes.body: Choirs of boys and unmarried girls sang hymns at Roman religious festivals. The Trojans treat the arrival of the horse as a holy procession.

questions: How does Virgil present the horse as a living, threatening creature in lines 237–240?
What warnings do the Trojans ignore in lines 242–245, and why do you think they ignore them?
Why does Aeneas break off his story to cry out to Troy in lines 241–242? What is the effect?
